schema_notes.is_historical_867: True if the barony name is contemporarily attested as a settlement, fortress, or administrative unit by <= 867 CE.
schema_notes.natural_proper_name: True if the barony name directly adopts a specific proper hydronym, oronym, choronym, or named topographic feature (excluding directional/locator compounds).
schema_notes.older_name_by_867: Records attested pre-867 CE names for the same site or immediate predecessor when distinct from the barony name.

b_mao_darfur.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; traditional Arabic regional name for northern Darfur/Kordofan attested only in later Islamic and colonial-era accounts.
b_mao_darfur.etymology_analysis: Audited from in-game name Dár al-Ríh (Arabic Dār al-Rīḥ, 'Land/Abode of the Wind'), a traditional regional designation in northern Darfur and northern Kordofan. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Dâr-er-Rîch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Dâr-er-Rîch).

b_malha.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented only in modern colonial and post-colonial Sudanese geographical records.
b_malha.etymology_analysis: From Arabic al-Māliḥa ('the salty'), referring to the saline springs and volcanic crater lake in the Meidob region of North Darfur. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_kerker.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; recorded only in modern Sudanese geographical and ethnographic surveys.
b_kerker.etymology_analysis: Modern settlement name in western Sudan (Darfur/Nuba region) with no documented pre-867 CE written attestation or established etymology.

b_tagabo.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in 19th- and 20th-century geographical and geological surveys of North Darfur.
b_tagabo.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Tagabo Hills (also known as the Berti Hills or Kutum Volcanic Field) in North Darfur, Sudan. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_teiga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern geographical and archaeological surveys of North Darfur.
b_teiga.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Teiga Plateau (Jebel Teiga) in North Darfur, Sudan, a sandstone plateau associated with Midob oral traditions. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_dar_wona.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Arabic regional designation documented in later Darfur Sultanate and modern administrative records.
b_dar_wona.etymology_analysis: Audited from in-game name Dár al-Saíd (Arabic Dār al-Saʿīd), a directional/regional designation for southern Darfur. Excluded from natural proper names as a directional/qualifier compound; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Dâr-es-Saît
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Dâr-es-Saît).

b_kundi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern geographical and ecological records of South Darfur.
b_kundi.etymology_analysis: Named after Lake Kundi, an endorheic perennial lake in South Darfur near the Bahr al-Arab. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_hurayz.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; known only from modern Sudanese geographical records.

morphemes.translation: little fortress / guarded place (diminutive of ḥirz)

b_hurayz.etymology_analysis: Arabic diminutive toponym (Ḥurayz) in Darfur, Sudan. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_el_fasher.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1792 CE when Sultan Abd al-Rahman al-Rashid established his permanent court (fāshir) at Rahad Tendelti.

morphemes.translation: open court/square before the sultan's palace

b_el_fasher.etymology_analysis: Audited from in-game name El-Fasher (Arabic al-Fāshir, 'the royal court/forecourt'). Founded in 1792 CE by Sultan Abd al-Rahman al-Rashid, well after 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Tûrre
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: *El-Fasher* founded in **1792** by Sultan Abd al-Rahman al-Rashid as the mobile *fāshir* (court) of Darfur.. Resolved via **Turra** (`b_turra`, ancient Daju and Tunjur royal mountain stronghold in the Jebel Marra). $\rightarrow$ **Magistrat v.

b_turra.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; associated with Keira sultans of Darfur from the 16th–17th centuries CE and documented in 19th-century accounts.
b_turra.etymology_analysis: Audited from actual barony Turra (not the Tarr fallback Alptiginstat). Turra is the ancestral heartland of the Fur and burial site of Keira sultans in the northern Jebel Marra (16th–17th centuries CE), with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_masa_fasher.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; modern/post-18th-century Darfur toponym.
b_masa_fasher.etymology_analysis: Compound Darfur toponym incorporating Sudanese Arabic fāshir ('royal court/camp'), a term associated with the post-16th-century Darfur Sultanate. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_hileila.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; recorded only in modern Sudanese geographical surveys.
b_hileila.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic diminutive of ḥilla ('village/quarter'), common in modern Darfur and Kordofan settlement names. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_simiat.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern geographical and archaeological surveys of the Jebel Marra / North Darfur region.
b_simiat.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Simiat Hills in North Darfur, Sudan. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_el-obeid.first_mention_attestation: Modern city founded in 1821 CE by Ottoman-Egyptian forces after previously serving as an 18th-century caravan stop under the Musaba'at Kingdom.
b_el-obeid.etymology_analysis: Audited from actual barony El Obeid (Arabic al-Ubayyiḍ, 'the little white'; in-game county-seat fallback Kordofan is first attested in 1672 CE by Evliya Çelebi). Modern city founded in 1821 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Kordofân
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kordofân).

b_east_kordofan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; directional subdivision of Kordofan (region itself first attested in 1672 CE).
b_east_kordofan.etymology_analysis: Audited from actual barony East Kordofan (not the Tarr fallback Thietmarstat). Directional English compound of Kordofan; excluded from natural proper names as a directional compound. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_sidrah.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented only in modern Sudanese geographical records.
b_sidrah.etymology_analysis: From Arabic sidra ('jujube tree'), a common descriptive settlement name in North Kordofan. Excluded from natural proper names as a generic common noun; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_shatt.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern ethnographic and linguistic surveys of South Kordofan.

morphemes.translation: Daju subgroup and hill settlement area in South Kordofan

b_shatt.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Shatt people and Shatt Hills southwest of Kadugli in South Kordofan (in-game county-seat fallback South Kordofan is also post-867). No written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Sût-Kordofân
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Sût-Kordofân).

b_liguri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in 20th-century linguistic and ethnographic surveys of the Nuba Mountains.
b_liguri.etymology_analysis: Refers to the Liguri (Logorik), an Eastern Daju-speaking community in the Nuba Mountains of South Kordofan. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_central_kordofan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; directional subdivision of Kordofan (region first attested in 1672 CE).
b_central_kordofan.etymology_analysis: Audited from in-game name Central Kordofan. Directional/locator English compound; excluded from natural proper names. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Middel-Kordofân
current_repo_state.b_origin: Central savanna reach of the pre-867 Kordofan realm (in-game: Central Kordofan)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor Central Kordofan fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to Middel-Kordofân.

b_en-nahud.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented as a town in West Kordofan in 19th- and 20th-century Sudanese records.
b_en-nahud.etymology_analysis: Audited from actual barony En Nahud (Arabic al-Nuhūd; in-game county-seat fallback West Kordofan is also post-867). No written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: West-Kordofân
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (West-Kordofân).

b_west_kordofan.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; directional subdivision of Kordofan (region first attested in 1672 CE).
b_west_kordofan.etymology_analysis: Audited from actual barony West Kordofan (not the Tarr fallback Baldarîchmarct). Directional English compound; excluded from natural proper names. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Baldarîchmarct
current_repo_state.b_origin: Baldarîchmarct — Disambiguated capital foundation: Chartered market borough established by Baldarîch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_lagowa.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in modern Sudanese administrative and linguistic records.
b_lagowa.etymology_analysis: Town in West Kordofan (Arabic al-Laqāwa) near the Nuba Hills, home to a Dar Fur Daju dialect community. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_goz_beida.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; capital of the Sultanate of Dar Sila documented in 19th-century European and Arabic accounts.
b_goz_beida.etymology_analysis: Audited from actual barony Goz Beïda (Arabic Qūz Bayḍāʾ, 'the white sand dune'), capital of the Sultanate of Dar Sila in eastern Chad. Descriptive common-noun compound; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_dar_sila.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Daju sultanate in eastern Chad founded after the late-15th-century Daju migration from Darfur.
b_dar_sila.etymology_analysis: Arabic Dār Sīlā ('Land of Sila'), denoting the Daju sultanate and region in southeastern Chad. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_east_sila.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; directional subdivision of Dar Sila.
b_east_sila.etymology_analysis: Directional English compound of Sila (Dar Sila). Excluded from natural proper names as a directional compound; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_fellata.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Arabic/Kanuri ethnonym for Fulani migrants in Chad and Sudan attested in later medieval and early modern sources.
b_fellata.etymology_analysis: From Kanuri/Arabic Fallāta/Fellata, the ethnonym for Fulani (Fula) communities settled in Chad and Sudan. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_ngama.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented only in modern Chadian geographical records.
b_ngama.etymology_analysis: Town in Chad (Hadjer-Lamis / Chari-Baguirmi area). No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_lairi.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; recorded only in modern Chadian geographical gazetteers.
b_lairi.etymology_analysis: Settlement name in central/eastern Chad with no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_yao_fitri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; became the capital of the Bilala Sultanate of Fitri in the 17th century CE.
b_yao_fitri.etymology_analysis: Audited from actual barony Yao (b_yao_fitri; capital of the Bilala Sultanate of Fitri from the 17th century CE). No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_kouki.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; recorded only in modern Chadian geographical gazetteers.
b_kouki.etymology_analysis: Settlement in central Chad (Fitri/Batha region) with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_gasga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; recorded only in modern Chadian geographical gazetteers.
b_gasga.etymology_analysis: Settlement in central Chad (Fitri/Batha region) with no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_ghazzal.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; Arabic name for the dry riverbed in central Chad documented in later Islamic and colonial geography.
b_ghazzal.etymology_analysis: Audited from in-game name Ghazzal (Arabic Baḥr al-Ghazāl, 'River/Sea of the Gazelle'), a major ephemeral wadi running northeast from Lake Chad toward the Bodélé Depression. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_wagna.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; recorded only in modern Chadian geographical gazetteers.
b_wagna.etymology_analysis: Settlement name in central Chad with no documented written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_manga.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; associated with Kanuri-speaking Manga groups and settlements in the Chad Basin documented in later centuries.
b_manga.etymology_analysis: Toponym in the Chad Basin associated with the Kanuri-speaking Manga. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_kadam.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; documented in Wadai/eastern Chad traditions and modern geographical surveys.
b_kadam.etymology_analysis: Refers to Mount Kadam / Kadama in the Wadai highlands of eastern Chad (noted in Wadai history before the capital moved to Wara). No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_kadam-west.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; modern directional compound based on Kadam.
b_kadam-west.etymology_analysis: Audited from in-game name Kadam-West. Directional English compound; excluded from natural proper names. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: West-Kadâm
current_repo_state.b_origin: Western slopes of the pre-867 Mount Kadam massif (in-game: Kadam-West)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Colonial English descriptor Kadam-West fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; standardized to West-Kadâm.

b_kadam-south.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; modern directional compound based on Kadam.
b_kadam-south.etymology_analysis: Audited from actual barony Kadam-South (not the Tarr fallback Goukounistat). Directional English compound; excluded from natural proper names. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_wara.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1635 CE by Abd al-Karim as the capital of the Wadai Sultanate (Ouaddai Empire).
b_wara.etymology_analysis: Audited from actual barony Ouara/Wara (b_wara), built c. 1635 CE by Abd al-Karim as the capital of the Wadai Sultanate and abandoned in the 19th century when its wells dried up. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_abeche.first_mention_attestation: Became the capital of the Wadai Sultanate around 1850 CE under Sultan Muhammad Sharif after Ouara's wells dried up.
b_abeche.etymology_analysis: City in eastern Chad (Arabic Absha) that replaced Ouara as capital of the Wadai Sultanate around 1850 CE. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_wadai.first_mention_attestation: Wadai Sultanate founded around 1635 CE by Abd al-Karim (preceded by a 16th-century non-Muslim kingdom).
b_wadai.etymology_analysis: Audited from actual barony Wadai (not the Tarr fallback Adamkirchen). Regional choronym (Arabic Waddāy / French Ouaddaï) for the eastern Chadian highlands and sultanate founded c. 1635 CE. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Adamkirchen
current_repo_state.b_origin: Torfukirchen — Disambiguated capital foundation: Parish collegiate church founded by Adam
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_ain_farah.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; ruined Tunjur capital (c. 13th–16th centuries CE) known from archaeology and later oral/historical accounts.
b_ain_farah.etymology_analysis: Audited from in-game name Ayn Farah (Arabic ʿAyn Faraḥ, 'Spring of Joy'), an archaeological site and spring in the Furnung mountains of North Darfur associated with the Tunjur ruler Shau Dorshid. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Aîn-Farâch
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Aîn-Farâch).

b_kubayh.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; major Darfur Sultanate caravan town on the Darb el-Arba'in from the 17th–19th centuries CE.
b_kubayh.etymology_analysis: Deserted oasis town (Kobbei / Kubayh) in North Darfur, peak trading hub of the Darfur Sultanate in the 18th–19th centuries CE along the Darb el-Arba'in route to Asyut. No written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_uri.first_mention_attestation: Unattested in contemporary written sources <= 867 CE; early Tunjur capital in northern Darfur with stone ruins and a mosque dated archaeologically to c. 1200 CE or later.
b_uri.etymology_analysis: Ruined walled city in northern Darfur, first capital of the Tunjur kingdom before Ain Farah. Archaeological remains date from c. 1200 CE onward; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_masalit.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE; the Masalit sultanate and homeland in western Darfur enter documentary records in the modern era (late 19th to early 20th century, e.g., 1903–1908 conflicts with Darfur Sultan Ali Dinar).
b_masalit.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ethnonym of the Masalit, a Nilo-Saharan (Maban-speaking) people of West Darfur and eastern Chad (Dar Masalit).

current_repo_state.name: Masalît
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Masalît).

b_wadi_azwa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Wadi Azum is a seasonal watercourse in western/central Darfur documented only in modern geographical and colonial-era surveys.
b_wadi_azwa.etymology_analysis: Arabic wādī ('seasonal river valley') combined with the local proper hydronym Azwa (modern Wadi Azum), draining western Darfur.

b_kabkabiya.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Fur dynastic tradition attributes its naming to a victory over Wadai during the reign of Sultan Ahmad Bukr (c. 1700–1720 CE), and it is documented as a caravan station under the Darfur Sultanate prior to 1898.
b_kabkabiya.etymology_analysis: According to Fur tradition, the name derives from the Fur phrase kebi kebbia ('they threw away their shields'), commemorating a Darfuri victory over Wadai under Ahmad Bukr (c. 1700–1720).

b_tureiq.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; both Tureiq and the in-game name Qimr (Dar Qimr / Kimr, centered at Kulbus in West Darfur) appear only in late precolonial and modern Sudanic/colonial records.
b_tureiq.etymology_analysis: The in-game barony name Qimr (repo 'Kîmer') refers to the Kimr/Gimr (Dar Qimr), a Taman-speaking group in West Darfur and Chad; Tureiq is a local Sudanese Arabic toponym.

current_repo_state.name: Kîmer
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kîmer).

b_qimr.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Dar Qimr (Kimr/Gimr) is documented only in late precolonial and modern Darfur/Chad records.
b_qimr.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kimr (Gimr/Qimr) ethnic group of West Darfur and eastern Chad, who speak a dialect of Taman.

b_tama.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Tama people and Sultanate of Tama along the Chad–Darfur borderland are attested only in later precolonial and modern accounts.
b_tama.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ethnonym of the Tama people, a Nilo-Saharan (Taman-speaking) community inhabiting eastern Chad and western Darfur.

b_umm_gafala.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Umm Gafala (and the in-game/repo label East Darfur) has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_umm_gafala.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic toponymic compound with umm ('mother of', common in Sudanese place names); the repo state maps it to 'Ôst-Dârfûr' (in-game: East Darfur).

current_repo_state.name: Ôst-Dârfûr
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Ôst-Dârfûr).

b_ghubaysh.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Ghubaysh (in West Kordofan / eastern Darfur borderland) is documented only in modern Sudanese administrative and historical records.
b_ghubaysh.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic toponym (غبيش), related to the diminutive pattern from ghabash ('dust-colored / twilight').

b_umm_kedada.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Umm Keddada in North Darfur appears only in modern Sudanese geographical and administrative records.
b_umm_kedada.etymology_analysis: Sudanese Arabic compound toponym (أم كدادة) formed with umm ('mother of / place of').

b_east_darfur.first_mention_attestation: East Darfur State was created in January 2012 (capital Ed Daein); no written attestation <= 867 CE exists for East Darfur or the repo's ahistorical 'Wiltrudstat' label.
b_east_darfur.etymology_analysis: Directional compound ('East Darfur', Arabic Sharq Dārfūr) created in 2012 from Dār Fūr ('abode of the Fur'); the repo state substitutes an ahistorical German-style name 'Wiltrudstat'.

current_repo_state.name: Wiltrudstat
current_repo_state.b_origin: Wiltrudstat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Wiltrud
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_gobir.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Hausa oral tradition places Gobir's foundation in the 11th–12th century CE, and contemporary external written accounts appear only in the later medieval/early modern period.

morphemes.translation: proper name of the Hausa city-state

b_gobir.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Hausa polity name for one of the seven Hausa Bakwai states, historically centered at Alkalawa and later Tibiri/Sabon Birni.

current_repo_state.name: Gobir
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Gobir).

b_gobir-east.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; both the in-game directional compound 'Gobir-East' and the repo's Rima River ('Rîme') reference lack any documentary attestation <= 867 CE.
b_gobir-east.etymology_analysis: In-game directional compound of Gobir ('Gobir-East'); the repo state maps it to 'Rîme' (Rima River), neither of which is attested in writing <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Rîme
current_repo_state.b_origin: Ancient pre-867 Rima River basin in Hausaland (in-game: Gobir-East)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Administrative sector Gobir-East fails Burden of Proof on Antiquity; resolved to ancient Rima river basin.

b_konni.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Birni-N'Konni in southern Niger is documented only in precolonial Hausa/Fulani-era and modern records.
b_konni.etymology_analysis: Hausa compound birnin ('walled city of') + Konni, a historic Hausa border town in Niger's Tahoua Region.

b_tahoua.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Tahoua in Niger is documented in late precolonial and French colonial records (e.g., early 20th-century colonial cercle).
b_tahoua.etymology_analysis: Settlement name in the Ader region of Niger (Hausa/Tuareg contact zone), serving as the modern capital of Tahoua Region.

current_repo_state.name: Tahoue
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Tahoue).

b_ader.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Ader region (a former province of the Sultanate of Aïr, which was founded in the 15th century) is attested only in post-medieval and modern sources.
b_ader.etymology_analysis: Regional choronym (Ader / Adar) for the plateau and valley landscape around Ader Doutchi in south-central Niger.

b_matankari.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Matankari (historic capital of Arewa in southwestern Niger) is documented only in precolonial oral/later written and colonial-era records.
b_matankari.etymology_analysis: Hausa settlement name in the Dallol Maouri valley of Niger, historically the seat of the Arewa polity prior to colonial relocation.

b_fika.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Bole tradition traces the Fika Emirate to the 15th century, with the move from Daniski to the current Fika town dated to 1805 CE.
b_fika.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the Bole-speaking Fika Emirate in Yobe State, northeastern Nigeria, established at its present site in 1805.

current_repo_state.name: Fike
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Fike).

b_gombe.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Gombe Emirate was founded in 1804 CE by Buba Yero during the Sokoto jihad (initially at Gombe Abba, later moved to Gombe Doma in 1919).
b_gombe.etymology_analysis: Name of the Fulani emirate founded in 1804 CE by Buba Yero in northeastern Nigeria.

b_gongola.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Gongola River in northeastern Nigeria is documented only in 19th-century and modern geographical records.
b_gongola.etymology_analysis: Indigenous hydronym of the Gongola River, the principal tributary of the Benue River in northeastern Nigeria.

b_yerwa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Yerwa was founded in 1907 CE by Abubakar Garbai of Borno on the site of the village of Kalwa, and the in-game name Kagha (Kaga, Borno State) likewise lacks pre-867 written attestation.
b_yerwa.etymology_analysis: Kanuri name Yerwa ('goodness/prosperity') given to the new Bornu capital founded in 1907; the repo state maps it to 'Kaghe' (in-game: Kagha, cf. Kaga LGA in Borno).

current_repo_state.name: Kaghe
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kaghe).

b_galaga.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Galaga (a minor locality in the Borno/Kaga area of northeastern Nigeria) has no pre-867 documentary record.
b_galaga.etymology_analysis: Local settlement toponym in the Borno region of northeastern Nigeria without documented pre-867 written history.

b_biu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Babur/Bura tradition dates the Biu Kingdom to c. 1670 CE under Mari Watila Tampta, with modern Biu town becoming the capital in 1878 CE.
b_biu.etymology_analysis: Originally called Viu in the Babur/Bura language, meaning 'high', referring to the elevated Biu Plateau town in Borno State.

b_margi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Marghi (Margi) people of Borno and Adamawa are documented only in later precolonial and modern ethnographic/historical sources.
b_margi.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ethnonym of the Marghi (Margi), a Chadic-speaking people of northeastern Nigeria and adjacent Cameroon/Chad.

b_daura.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Daura appears in retrospective Hausa oral/chronicle traditions (the Bayajidda legend) and later medieval/early modern Arabic and Hausa writings.

morphemes.translation: proper name of the city and emirate

b_daura.etymology_analysis: Historic Hausa city-state in Katsina State, northern Nigeria, traditionally associated in Hausa legend with Queen Daurama and Bayajidda.

current_repo_state.name: Daure
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Daure).

b_zinder.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Zinder rose to prominence as the capital of the Sultanate of Damagaram in the mid-18th century CE.
b_zinder.etymology_analysis: Name of the historic city in southern Niger (known locally as Damagaram), which became a major Sahelian center in the 18th–19th centuries.

b_kano.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the 19th-century Kano Chronicle traces Kano's first king Bagauda to 999 CE, and contemporary external written attestations begin in the late medieval/early modern period.

morphemes.translation: proper name of the city and kingdom

b_kano.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Hausa name for the major Hausa city-state centered around Dala Hill in northern Nigeria.

current_repo_state.name: Kanô
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kanô).

b_hadejia.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Hadejia (formerly Biram, one of the Hausa Bakwai) was transformed into a Fulani emirate in 1808 CE and lacks pre-867 written records.
b_hadejia.etymology_analysis: Hausa town and emirate in Jigawa State, northern Nigeria, historically linked to the Hausa Bakwai state of Biram.

b_kufan_kanawa.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kufan Kanawa in Niger's Zinder Region is an archaeological walled-settlement site studied via modern ethnoarchaeology and Hausa oral tradition.
b_kufan_kanawa.etymology_analysis: Hausa phrase meaning 'ruins of the Kano people', an archaeological walled site in southern Niger linked in oral tradition to early Hausa/Kano origins.

b_katagum.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Katagum was founded in 1814 CE by Malam Zaki during the Sokoto jihad and visited by Hugh Clapperton and Walter Oudney in 1824 CE.
b_katagum.etymology_analysis: Toponym of the Katagum Emirate in Bauchi State, northeastern Nigeria, established in 1814 CE on the Jama'are River.

current_repo_state.name: Katagum
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Katagum).

b_azare.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Azare was founded in early 1814 CE by Malam Zaki (appointed by Usman dan Fodio) and became the seat of Katagum Emirate in 1916 CE.
b_azare.etymology_analysis: Name of the town in Bauchi State, Nigeria, founded by Malam Zaki in 1814 CE.

b_kudu.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kudu (or Birnin Kudu in Jigawa State) has no contemporary documentary attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kudu.etymology_analysis: Hausa directional noun kudu ('south'), used in northern Nigerian place names such as Birnin Kudu ('walled town of the south').

b_gabas.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Gabas (cf. Garun Gabas / Garin Gabas in Jigawa State, associated with Biram) has no contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_gabas.etymology_analysis: Hausa directional noun gabas ('east'), appearing in northern Nigerian place names such as Garun Gabas.

b_rano.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Rano is remembered in Hausa tradition as one of the seven Hausa Bakwai states, without contemporary written records <= 867 CE.
b_rano.etymology_analysis: Historic Hausa settlement and emirate name in southern Kano State, northern Nigeria.

current_repo_state.name: Ranô
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Ranô).

b_kura.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Kura in Kano State is mentioned in later Kano traditions (e.g., subjugation under Sarkin Kano Naguji, r. 1194–1247 CE in the 19th-century Kano Chronicle).
b_kura.etymology_analysis: Hausa toponym in Kano State (homophonous with Hausa kūra, 'hyena').

b_kaduna.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the city of Kaduna was founded by British colonists in 1900 CE on the Kaduna River.
b_kaduna.etymology_analysis: Named after the Kaduna River, whose name derives from the Hausa plural kadduna ('crocodiles'), referring to the crocodiles inhabiting the river.

current_repo_state.name: Kadune
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kadune).

b_turunku.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Turunku is attested in Zazzau chronicles and oral traditions as the earlier capital of Zazzau prior to Bakwa Turunku's move to Zaria in the 16th century CE.

morphemes.translation: proper name of the ancient hill settlement

b_turunku.etymology_analysis: Indigenous toponym of the rocky hill-settlement south of Zaria that served as an early capital of the Kingdom of Zazzau.

b_katsina.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; tradition dates Katsina's foundation to c. 1100 CE, and contemporary written records appear only in the later medieval/early modern period.

morphemes.translation: proper name of the city and kingdom

b_katsina.etymology_analysis: Historic Hausa city-state (one of the Hausa Bakwai) in northern Nigeria; local tradition links the name to Katsina, wife of legendary founder Kumayo.

current_repo_state.name: Katzine
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Katzine).

b_marandi.first_mention_attestation: First attested in writing in 872 CE by the Arab geographer al-Ya'qubi (Tarikh) as Maranda, and later by al-Mas'udi, Ibn al-Faqih, Ibn Hawqal, and al-Idrisi; this is 5 years after the 867 CE baseline.

morphemes.translation: caravan station and oasis settlement name

b_marandi.etymology_analysis: Recorded as Maranda in early Arabic geographies from 872 CE onward, identified with the archaeological and modern settlement of Marandet (Tuareg Mărăndat) southwest of Agadez in Niger.

b_zazzau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the 20th-century Chronicle of Zaria places Zazzau's regnal list back to 1010 CE, while the in-game name Zaria was founded in the 16th century CE (c. 1536) by Bakwa Turunku.
b_zazzau.eponym_details: The in-game barony name Zaria (repo 'Sarje') was named in the 16th century (c. 1536 CE) after Zaria, the second daughter of Zazzau ruler Bakwa Turunku.
b_zazzau.etymology_analysis: Zazzau (also Zegzeg) is the historic Hausa kingdom name; the in-game name Zaria was coined in the 16th century after Bakwa Turunku's daughter Zaria.

current_repo_state.name: Sarje
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Sarje).

b_gusau.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Gusau emerged as a significant town in Zamfara in the 19th to early 20th century (colonial-era administrative/railway hub from 1907 onward).
b_gusau.etymology_analysis: Hausa settlement name in Zamfara State, northwestern Nigeria, now the state capital.

b_kebbi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; the Kingdom of Kebbi rose to prominence in the early 16th century CE under Kanta Kotal.
b_kebbi.etymology_analysis: Name of the historic Hausa-speaking Kingdom of Kebbi (Kabi) along the Rima/Sokoto valley in northwestern Nigeria.

current_repo_state.name: Kebbi
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kebbi).

b_gummi.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Gummi in Zamfara State is documented only in precolonial Sokoto-era and modern Nigerian records.
b_gummi.etymology_analysis: Hausa town name in Zamfara State, northwestern Nigeria.

b_sokoto-north.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE; Sokoto was transformed from a semi-permanent camp into a walled city in 1809 CE by Muhammed Bello, son of Usman dan Fodio.

morphemes.translation: city name (from Arabic sūq, 'market' / local name)

b_sokoto-north.etymology_analysis: Directional compound ('Sokoto-North') from Sokoto, the capital of the Sokoto Caliphate founded in 1809 CE by Muhammed Bello.

b_sokoto.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1809 CE as a ribat (frontier military camp) by Muhammad Bello, son of Usman dan Fodio, becoming the capital of the Sokoto Caliphate; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_sokoto.etymology_analysis: Modern Sokoto is an anglicization of the local Hausa name Sakkwato, derived from Arabic sūq ('market').

current_repo_state.name: Sokotô
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Sokotô).

b_dutsi.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Dutsi is recorded in later Hausa tradition as an early capital of the Kingdom of Zamfara (traditionally 11th century CE) and is a modern town and LGA in Katsina State, Nigeria.
b_dutsi.etymology_analysis: From Hausa dutsi (variant of dutse), meaning 'rock' or 'stone', a generic common noun.

b_anka.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Anka became the capital of the Kingdom of Zamfara in the second half of the 19th century CE after Birnin Zamfara was destroyed by Gobir.
b_anka.etymology_analysis: Indigenous Hausa settlement name in Zamfara State, Nigeria; no verified pre-867 CE etymology.

b_zuru.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Zuru is a town and traditional emirate headquarters in southern Kebbi State, Nigeria, inhabited by the Lelna (Dakarkari) and neighboring peoples.
b_zuru.etymology_analysis: Local toponym in southern Kebbi State, Nigeria; no verified pre-867 CE documentary etymology.

b_yauri.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Its first capital, Bin Yauri (Birnin Yauri), was founded in the early 16th century CE (or traditionally 1411 CE) by the 5th Sarki of Gungu Kafa.
b_yauri.eponym_details: Named after Yauri, the 5th Sarki (ruler) of Gungu Kafa (Gungawa), who founded Bin Yauri in the early 16th century CE.
b_yauri.etymology_analysis: Named after the 5th Sarki of Gungu Kafa in the early 16th century CE; local tradition also links the name to the fish trade along the Niger River.

current_repo_state.name: Jauri
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Jauri).

b_kontokoro.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Kontokoro (Kotonkoro) is a modern town and district in Mariga LGA, Niger State, Nigeria.
b_kontokoro.etymology_analysis: Local Nigerian settlement name in Mariga LGA, Niger State; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

b_ulaira.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Ulaira is an archaeological site in the Kainji Lake (Middle Niger) region of Nigeria investigated in the 1980s for first-millennium CE potsherd pavements.
b_ulaira.etymology_analysis: Modern archaeological site name in the Kainji Lake basin, Nigeria; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_bauchi.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the early 19th century CE (1800–1810 CE, c. 1809) by Yakubu dan Dadi as the capital of the Bauchi Emirate; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bauchi.eponym_details: Named after Baushe, a hunter who settled in the area and advised Yakubu dan Dadi where to build the city in the early 19th century CE.
b_bauchi.etymology_analysis: According to local tradition, named after the hunter Baushe, who inhabited the site prior to Yakubu dan Dadi's foundation of the Bauchi Emirate (1800–1810 CE).

current_repo_state.name: Bautschi
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Bautschi).

b_durum.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Durum is a village north of Bauchi in Bauchi State, Nigeria, near the modern Bauchi State Airport.
b_durum.etymology_analysis: Local village name in Bauchi State, Nigeria; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

b_jos.first_mention_attestation: Established in the early 20th century CE (tin-mining activities began 1902–1904) under British colonial rule on the Jos Plateau; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_jos.etymology_analysis: Early 20th-century colonial mining settlement on the Jos Plateau; its exact etymology (variously linked to Berom or Hausa mispronunciations) remains debated.

b_gbagye.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Gbagye (Gbagyi, Gbari, or Gwari) is an ethnonym for an indigenous people of central Nigeria rather than a documented pre-867 CE settlement.
b_gbagye.etymology_analysis: Derived from the ethnonym of the Gbagyi (Gwari) people of central Nigeria.

b_keffi.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1802 CE by the Fulani warrior-leader Abdu Zanga in Nasarawa State, central Nigeria; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_keffi.etymology_analysis: Town in Nasarawa State founded c. 1802 CE; the name Keffi (Hausa kafi) is associated with a fortified stockade/encampment.

current_repo_state.name: Keffi
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Keffi).

b_moda.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Moda is a modern village name in northeastern Nigeria (e.g., Moda in Michika, Adamawa State).
b_moda.etymology_analysis: Local Nigerian settlement name; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

b_wase.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Wase was founded in the early 19th century CE during the Sokoto Jihad by Madaki Hassan's father and formalized as an emirate under Malam Yakubu of Bauchi.
b_wase.etymology_analysis: Early 19th-century Fulani emirate town built on the northern side of Wase Rock in Plateau State, Nigeria.

b_kwararafa.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Kwararafa (Kororofa) was a Benue Valley confederacy flourishing between the 15th and 19th centuries CE, first mentioned in late 15th/16th-century external accounts (such as Leo Africanus and Bornu/Kano chronicles).
b_kwararafa.etymology_analysis: Hausa exonym (Kororofa) for the Jukun-led Benue Valley state; scholars (e.g., C. K. Meek) derive it from Kororo-afa ('the salt people'), Kwana Apa, Kuru Apa, or Apa of the Kworra (river).

current_repo_state.name: Kwararafe
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Kwararafe).

b_wukari.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Wukari emerged as the seat of the Aku Uka (Jukun federation) in the 18th–19th centuries CE (documented in 1780 CE Lafia traditions and consolidating power in the 1840s after Kwararafa's decline).
b_wukari.etymology_analysis: Jukun town and traditional capital of the Wukari Federation in Taraba State, Nigeria; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

b_muri.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1817 CE as a Fulbe jihad emirate by Hamman Ruwa in Taraba State, Nigeria; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_muri.etymology_analysis: Fulbe emirate and town established in 1817 CE in the Benue Valley (Taraba State, Nigeria).

b_gazargamo.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the second half of the 15th century CE (c. 1460–1488 CE, commonly dated c. 1472 CE) by Mai Ali I Gaji as the permanent capital of the Bornu Empire; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_gazargamo.etymology_analysis: Kanuri Birni Gazargamo (Hausaized as Ngazargamu), literally 'walled city of Ngazargamu'; proposed etymologies link Ngazar to the earlier N'gasar/N'gizim inhabitants and gamu to a monarch/spirit, or interpret the compound as 'the secure city' or 'city of kings'.

current_repo_state.name: Gasargamu
current_repo_state.b_origin: Historic Kanem-Bornu capital Birni Gazargamo (in-game: Gasargamu)
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic Historic Capital.

b_gambaru.first_mention_attestation: No written attestation <= 867 CE. Gambaru (near Ngazargamu) is documented in the late 16th century CE by chronicler Ahmad ibn Fartuwa (1571–1583 CE) as the brick palace residence of Mai Idris Alooma; modern Gamboru Ngala is on the Cameroon border.
b_gambaru.etymology_analysis: Kanuri settlement and royal palace name in Borno, Nigeria; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

b_diakam.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Unattested in early documentary sources for Bornu or Kanem.
b_diakam.etymology_analysis: Minor or unattested Borno/Kanem toponym with no verified pre-867 CE etymology.

b_garumele.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Garumele (Garoumélé) in Diffa Region, Niger, is a medieval walled fired-brick site associated with Kanem-Bornu's 14th–15th century CE transition prior to Ngazargamu.
b_garumele.etymology_analysis: Kanuri toponym containing garu ('wall, fortified town') for the medieval brick site in southeastern Niger; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

current_repo_state.name: Garumêle
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Garumêle).

b_ajere.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Ajere is an archaeological/settlement site in the Komadugu Yobe valley of Borno/Yobe, Nigeria, studied alongside Yau and Birnin Gazargamo.
b_ajere.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in the Komadugu Yobe valley, northeastern Nigeria; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

b_balbelec.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Unattested in early documentary sources for Bornu or Niger.
b_balbelec.etymology_analysis: Minor or unattested Borno/Niger toponym with no verified pre-867 CE etymology.

b_gaskeru.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Gaskeru (Gueskérou) is a modern rural commune in Diffa Department, Diffa Region, southeastern Niger.
b_gaskeru.etymology_analysis: Local Kanuri/Nigerien settlement name (French spelling Gueskérou) along the Komadugu Yobe; no pre-867 CE etymology.

b_diffa.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Diffa is a modern city and regional capital in southeastern Niger on the Komadugu Yobe.
b_diffa.etymology_analysis: Modern city and region name in southeastern Niger; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

b_munio.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Munio (Mounio) is a historical region and former province of the Bornu Empire in modern southern Niger.
b_munio.etymology_analysis: Historical Bornu province name in southern Niger; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

current_repo_state.name: Mûnjô
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Mûnjô).

b_zamtam.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Zamtam is recorded in later Bornu dynastic chronicles (Girgam) as the place in Bornu where Mai Dunama II Dibalemi died c. 1259 CE.
b_zamtam.etymology_analysis: Historical Bornu toponym attested in connection with 13th-century CE Sayfawa history; no pre-867 CE etymology.

b_nguru.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Nguru in Yobe State, Nigeria, probably dates from around the 15th century CE.
b_nguru.etymology_analysis: Kanuri town name near the Hadejia River in Yobe State, Nigeria, dating from c. 15th century CE.

b_yau.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Yau (Yo) is a settlement and archaeological site in the Komadugu Yobe valley near Lake Chad excavated by Graham Connah.
b_yau.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in the Komadugu Yobe valley, Borno/Yobe, Nigeria; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

current_repo_state.name: Jâu
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Jâu).

b_kukawa.first_mention_attestation: Founded in 1814 CE as Kuka by Muhammad al-Amin al-Kanemi, becoming the capital of the Kanem–Bornu Empire in 1846–1893 CE; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kukawa.etymology_analysis: Founded in 1814 CE as Kuka (named after a baobab tree, kuka, a generic common noun), later known as Kukawa.

b_garu_kime.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Garu Kime is a late Bornu fired-brick archaeological site at Monguno, Borno State, Nigeria, associated in chronicles with a 15th-century CE royal residence prior to Ngazargamu.
b_garu_kime.etymology_analysis: Kanuri compound meaning 'red wall', referring to the fired-brick ruins at Monguno, Borno State, Nigeria.

b_dikwa.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Dikwa in Borno State, Nigeria, rose to prominence as the capital of Rabih az-Zubayr in 1893 CE and of German Borno (Dikwa Emirate) in 1902 CE.
b_dikwa.etymology_analysis: Kanuri town name in Borno State, Nigeria; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

b_mege.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Mege is a settlement mound on the firki clay plains near Daima, Borno State, Nigeria, excavated archaeologically by Detlef Gronenborn.
b_mege.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name on the firki plains south of Lake Chad; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

b_jimi.first_mention_attestation: First recorded in written texts from the 12th century CE (al-Idrīsī, 1154 CE), though later traditions place its origins as Kanem's capital earlier; no contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_jimi.etymology_analysis: Medieval capital of the Kanem Empire east of Lake Chad, first attested in 12th-century CE Arabic geography.

current_repo_state.name: Dschîmi
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Authentic pre-867 indigenous physical toponym and territorial catchment (Dschîmi).

b_tie.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Tié is a fired-brick archaeological site in central Kanem, Chad (thermoluminescence-dated to c. 1110 ± 80 CE), tentatively proposed as the site of Njimi.
b_tie.etymology_analysis: Modern Chadian toponym for a medieval fired-brick enclosure in central Kanem; no written attestation <= 867 CE.

b_tarazki.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Tarazki is mentioned in post-867 CE Arabic geographical accounts of medieval Kanem alongside Manan.
b_tarazki.etymology_analysis: Medieval town name in Kanem recorded in post-867 CE Arabic geographical literature; etymology uncertain.

b_madan.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Unattested in early documentary sources for Kanem or Bornu.
b_madan.etymology_analysis: Minor or unattested Kanem/Bornu toponym with no verified pre-867 CE etymology.

b_auno.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Auno is a town in Konduga LGA, Borno State, Nigeria, located west of Maiduguri.
b_auno.etymology_analysis: Local town name in Borno State, Nigeria; no documented pre-867 CE etymology.

b_manan.first_mention_attestation: First described in contemporary written sources by al-Idrīsī in 1154 CE as the pre-Islamic/early capital of Kanem; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_manan.etymology_analysis: Early capital of Kanem recorded by al-Idrīsī (1154 CE, sometimes spelled Matan); its exact location and etymology remain uncertain.

current_repo_state.name: Manân
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Resolved via verified historical center Manân documented in tarraconian_titles_1059.md.

b_nguigmi.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. N'Guigmi is a town on the former northwestern shore of Lake Chad in Diffa Region, Niger.
b_nguigmi.etymology_analysis: From Kanuri n'jié kimé, meaning 'large red clay pot'.

b_kanem.first_mention_attestation: First attested in contemporary written sources in 872 CE by al-Yaʿqūbī (Taʾrīkh), who mentions the kingdom of the Zaghawa living in Kānim; while retrospective dynastic traditions (Girgam) place its origin c. 700 CE, no written attestation <= 867 CE exists.
b_kanem.etymology_analysis: Derived from anem ('south') in Teda and Kanuri, a directional geographic term referring to the region south of the Sahara / Fezzan.

b_kagusti.first_mention_attestation: No contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE. Unattested in early documentary sources for Kanem or Chad.
b_kagusti.etymology_analysis: Minor or unattested Kanem toponym with no verified pre-867 CE etymology.

b_massenya.first_mention_attestation: Founded in the first half of the 16th century CE (c. 1522 CE) as the historical capital of the Sultanate of Bagirmi in Chad (first mentioned in a Bornu chronicle in 1578 CE as Bakarmi); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_massenya.etymology_analysis: Historical capital of the Sultanate of Bagirmi founded in the early 16th century CE; no pre-867 CE etymology.

b_baguirmi-west.first_mention_attestation: Unoccupied directional sub-barony derived from Baguirmi (first attested in 1578 CE as 'Bakarmi' in a Bornu chronicle); no contemporary written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_baguirmi-west.etymology_analysis: Directional compound ('Baguirmi-West') formed from the regional/state name Baguirmi plus the English locator '-west'; excluded from natural proper names as a directional compound.

b_baguirmi.first_mention_attestation: First mentioned in a Bornu chronicle (Ahmad ibn Furtu) in 1578 CE as 'Bakarmi'; Bagirmi oral tradition places the state's foundation at Massenya around 1522 CE (or 1493 CE).
b_baguirmi.etymology_analysis: Audited as Baguirmi (Sultanate of Bagirmi, capital Massenya) rather than the repo's synthetic disambiguated label 'Idrisstat'. Attested in 1578 CE as 'Bakarmi'; the name denotes the Barma-led Bagirmi state southeast of Lake Chad.

current_repo_state.name: Idrisstat
current_repo_state.b_origin: Idrisstat — Disambiguated capital foundation: Municipal foundation chartered by Idris
current_repo_state.b_anachronism: Disambiguated intra-county capital barony.

b_biddiri.first_mention_attestation: Historical center of Fulani Islamic scholars (faki) located 10 km from Massenya, documented in Bagirmi traditions and 19th-century European/modern historiography; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_biddiri.etymology_analysis: Settlement of Fulani Islamic scholars near Massenya in Baguirmi, Chad, attested in post-1500 Bagirmi-Fulani history and 19th-century accounts.

b_banre.first_mention_attestation: Riverine population/settlement along the Chari River in Baguirmi, recorded in historiography as subjugated and Islamized under Mbang Adji Mohammed el-Amine (r. 1741–1784 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_banre.etymology_analysis: Toponym and ethnonym for a Chari River community in the Baguirmi sphere, documented only in post-18th-century historical accounts.

b_migri.first_mention_attestation: Settlement in Baguirmi (later renamed Anja / Kut Anja) attested in 19th-century accounts as the site where Aahi Buulo's Fulani force was defeated by Mbang Burkumanda in the 1820s; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_migri.etymology_analysis: Historical Baguirmi settlement name (later Anja, then deserted as Kut Anja) recorded in 19th-century Chari-Baguirmi historiography.

b_logone-birni.first_mention_attestation: Founded around 1700 CE by Prince Bruha (with 'Logon' noted by Giovanni Lorenzo d'Anania in the 16th century); visited and described in writing by Dixon Denham on 23 January 1824 CE.
b_logone-birni.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Logone River name and Kanuri 'birni' ('walled town, fort'), meaning 'Fort Logone'; capital of the Southern Kotoko Kingdom.

b_barma2.first_mention_attestation: Autonym of the Bagirmi people of Chad (auditing barony b_barma2 rather than the erroneous repo fallback 'Tendukhede'); documented in post-1500 Bagirmi/Bornu history and 19th-century European/linguistic records, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_barma2.etymology_analysis: Audited as Barma (the autonym of the Bagirmi people of Chari-Baguirmi, Chad) rather than the repo's erroneous 'Tendukhede' fallback. No <= 867 CE written attestation exists.

b_dam_barma.first_mention_attestation: Chari River population/settlement ('Dam') in Baguirmi, recorded in historiography as subjugated and Islamized under Mbang Adji Mohammed el-Amine (r. 1741–1784 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_dam_barma.etymology_analysis: Local Chari-Baguirmi settlement/ethnonym paired with Barma in the barony key ('b_dam_barma'), attested only in post-18th-century Bagirmi historiography.

b_sarwa.first_mention_attestation: East Chadic language (Sarua/Sarwa) and community in southwestern Chad; documented only in 19th–20th century linguistic and ethnographic literature, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_sarwa.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and glossonym (Sarua/Sarwa) of an East Chadic-speaking community in southwestern Chad near the Chari River.

b_kwang.first_mention_attestation: East Chadic language and ethnic group (Kwang/Kwong) in southwestern Chad (auditing barony b_kwang rather than county-seat fallback 'Kuku'); documented only in 19th–20th century linguistic/ethnographic sources, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kwang.etymology_analysis: Audited as Kwang (East Chadic language and people of southwestern Chad) rather than the repo's county-seat fallback 'Kuku'. No <= 867 CE written attestation exists.

b_kim.first_mention_attestation: Mbum-group language and ethnic group inhabiting villages in southern Chad along the Logone River; documented in 19th-century Bagirmi/European accounts and 20th-century ethnography, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kim.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and language name of the Kim people of southern Chad (Mayo-Kebbi Est).

b_bousso.first_mention_attestation: Town on the Chari River in Chari-Baguirmi, Chad; documented in 19th–20th century European exploration and colonial records, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bousso.etymology_analysis: Toponym for the Chari River town of Bousso in south-central Chad (Loug Chari department).

b_masa.first_mention_attestation: Chadic ethnic group and language (Masa / Massa / Masana) in southern Chad and northern Cameroon; documented in 19th–20th century European and ethnographic sources, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_masa.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Masa (Massa/Masana) Chadic-speaking people of the Logone valley in Chad and Cameroon.

b_mbara.first_mention_attestation: Endangered Chadic (Biu–Mandara) language and community in Chad; documented in 20th-century linguistic literature (e.g., Tourneux, Seignobos & Lafarge 1986), with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_mbara.etymology_analysis: Glossonym and ethnonym for the Mbara-speaking community of Chad.

b_lafana.first_mention_attestation: Locality in the Chari-Baguirmi Region of Chad; appears only in modern geographical gazetteers and maps, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_lafana.etymology_analysis: Local settlement name in Chari-Baguirmi, Chad, lacking pre-modern documentary attestation.

b_tumak.first_mention_attestation: East Chadic language and people (Tumak/Toumak) in southwestern Chad (Moyen-Chari/Koumra); documented in 19th–20th century linguistic/ethnographic sources (e.g., Caprile 1975), with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_tumak.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and glossonym of the Tumak people of southwestern Chad.

b_miltou.first_mention_attestation: Town on the Chari River in Chad, famously referenced in the 1894 Franco-German colonial boundary agreement (linking the 14th meridian and Miltou); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_miltou.etymology_analysis: Settlement on the Chari River near Bousso, associated with the East Chadic Miltu (Gàlì) language.

b_sumray.first_mention_attestation: East Chadic language and people (Somrai/Sumray, autonym Sibine) in southwestern Chad; documented in 19th-century Bagirmi accounts and 20th-century linguistics, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_sumray.etymology_analysis: Exonym/ethnonym for the Sibine (Somrai/Sumray) East Chadic-speaking people of Tandjilé and Laï in Chad.

b_niellim.first_mention_attestation: Bua-speaking community along the Chari River in southern Chad that formed a small sultanate in the mid-19th century; documented in 19th–20th century sources, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_niellim.etymology_analysis: Historical name for the Lwaà (Niellim) Bua-speaking people and 19th-century sultanate along the Chari River.

b_dar_rashid.first_mention_attestation: Southeastern Chadian territory (Dâr Raschît) documented in 19th-century European exploration and Arab-Sudanic geography; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_dar_rashid.etymology_analysis: Arabic territorial compound 'Dār Rashīd' ('territory of Rashid'), following the Sudanic-Sahelian naming pattern for regional chiefdoms/territories.

b_boa.first_mention_attestation: Adamawa/Savanna language and ethnic group (Bua/Boa/Boua) north of the Chari River around Korbol and Gabil in Chad; documented in 19th–20th century ethnographic and linguistic sources, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_boa.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and glossonym of the Bua (Boa) people of south-central Chad.

b_melfi_sao.first_mention_attestation: Melfi (Guéra Region, Chad) is documented in late 19th-century French sources (Derendinger 1897) and became a French administrative subdivision in 1934; combined here with 'Sao'. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_melfi_sao.etymology_analysis: Compound of the Chadian town Melfi with the regional/civilizational qualifier '-Sao' (added for in-game disambiguation).

b_bogo.first_mention_attestation: Traditional Lamidat of Bogo in Diamaré (Far North Cameroon) founded in 1773 CE; Bogo is also recorded in 19th-century accounts (Heinrich Barth) as a Musgum-Fulani battle site. No written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bogo.etymology_analysis: Audited as Bogo (Diamaré Department, Cameroon) rather than the county-seat fallback 'Diamare'. Per Musgum tradition, 'Bogo' derives from a Musgum word meaning 'noise', commemorating a major battle.

b_mindif.first_mention_attestation: Town and Fulani lamidat in Far North Cameroon established in the early 19th century during the Sokoto/Adamawa jihad; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_mindif.etymology_analysis: Named after the nearby Mindif Peak (Dent de Mindif); per Musgum tradition, 'Mindif' literally means 'the mouth of man'.

b_kalfou.first_mention_attestation: Town and Fulani lamidat in Mayo-Danay (Far North Cameroon), settled by Fulani followers of Mama Adde in the 1820s–1840s; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kalfou.etymology_analysis: Town and commune in Far North Cameroon, historically a Fulani lamidat receiving its banner from Sokoto in the 19th century.

b_bindir.first_mention_attestation: Town and Fulani lamidat (Bindir/Binder) in Mayo-Kebbi Ouest, Chad, founded in the early 19th century under Modibbo Buba Bindir; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bindir.etymology_analysis: Historic Fulani lamidat and sub-prefecture in southwestern Chad (Mayo-Binder department).

b_gizey.first_mention_attestation: Western Masa dialect and community (Gizay/Gizey) spoken around Guéré in Far North Cameroon and adjacent Chad; documented in 20th-century linguistic literature, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_gizey.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and dialect name of the Western Masa (Gizay) community in the Cameroon-Chad borderland.

b_garoua.first_mention_attestation: Port city on the Benue River in northern Cameroon, established by the Fulani emir Modibbo Adama in the first half of the 19th century; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_garoua.etymology_analysis: Capital of Cameroon's North Region on the Benue River, founded by Modibbo Adama in the early 19th century.

b_bibemi.first_mention_attestation: Town and Fulani lamidat in Bénoué Department, North Region, Cameroon, founded in the early 19th century during the Fulani jihad; no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bibemi.etymology_analysis: Historic Fulani lamidat and commune in the Bénoué valley of northern Cameroon.

b_babur.first_mention_attestation: Hausa exonym ('Babur') for the Bura-Pabir Chadic ethnic group of northeastern Nigeria (Borno/Adamawa); documented in 19th–20th century colonial and ethnographic sources, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_babur.etymology_analysis: Hausa exonym for the Bura-Pabir people of Biu and Hawul in Borno State, northeastern Nigeria.

b_kera.first_mention_attestation: East Chadic language and ethnic group in southwestern Chad and northern Cameroon; documented in 20th-century linguistic literature (e.g., Karen Ebert), with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kera.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and glossonym of the Kera people of southwestern Chad and Far North Cameroon.

b_marba.first_mention_attestation: Chadic (Masa-branch) language and Azumeina ethnic group of southwestern Chad; documented in 20th-century linguistic and Bible-translation literature (e.g., Price 1968), with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_marba.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and glossonym of the Marba (one of the Azumeina clans) in Tandjilé, southwestern Chad.

b_ngambay.first_mention_attestation: Major Sara language and ethnic group (Sara Gambai) in southwestern Chad; documented in 19th–20th century colonial and linguistic sources, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ngambay.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym and language name of the Sara Gambai (Ngambay) people of southern Chad.

b_makari.first_mention_attestation: Audited as Makari/Makary (Kotoko city-state in Cameroon) rather than county-seat fallback 'Kotokô'. Mentioned in 16th-century written sources by Giovanni Lorenzo d'Anania (1573) and Bornu scholar Ahmad ibn Furtu (1578 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_makari.etymology_analysis: Audited as Makary (Makari), a major Kotoko city-state in the Chari delta; 'Makari' is also the Kanuri name for the Kotoko.

b_ngala.first_mention_attestation: Historic town in Borno State, Nigeria, documented in post-1500 Bornu chronicles and 19th-century accounts (Barth, Nachtigal); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_ngala.etymology_analysis: Historic settlement in eastern Borno State, Nigeria, near the Cameroon border and Lake Chad basin.

b_kousseri.first_mention_attestation: Kotoko city-state (founded/known indigenously as Mser) mentioned in 16th-century written sources by Giovanni Lorenzo d'Anania (1573) and Ahmad ibn Furtu (1578 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_kousseri.etymology_analysis: From Arabic 'quṣūr' ('palaces'), applied to the Kotoko city-state known indigenously as Mser at the confluence of the Chari and Logone rivers.

b_duolo.first_mention_attestation: Audited as Doulo (Dulo/Duolo), historical capital of the Mandara (Wandala) Kingdom from c. 1580 CE (Mandara itself first attested by Fra Mauro in 1459 CE); no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_duolo.etymology_analysis: Audited as Doulo (Duolo/Dulo), the 16th–19th century capital of the Wandala/Mandara Kingdom near Mora in Far North Cameroon, rather than the county-seat fallback 'Wandale'.

b_bama.first_mention_attestation: Town in Borno State, northeastern Nigeria (later seat of Dikwa Emirate and Bama Emirate); documented in modern/colonial-era sources, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_bama.etymology_analysis: Toponym for the town of Bama in Borno State, northeastern Nigeria.

b_dagwamba.first_mention_attestation: Ethnic group (Dagomba/Dagbamba) whose oral traditions recount a 13th-century migration from Lake Chad to northern Ghana; written attestations appear only in post-1500 chronicles and European accounts, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_dagwamba.etymology_analysis: Ethnonym of the Dagomba (Dagbamba) people, placed in Wandala in-game in reference to oral traditions of Lake Chad origins.

b_salamat.first_mention_attestation: Seasonally intermittent river (Bahr Salamat) and southeastern Chadian region; documented in 19th-century European exploration and 20th-century colonial administration (prefecture established 1960), with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_salamat.etymology_analysis: Named after the Bahr Salamat river (from Arabic 'baḥr' 'river/sea' + 'Salamat'), which gives its name to the Salamat region of southeastern Chad.

b_iro.first_mention_attestation: Cyclical endorheic lake (Lac Iro) in Moyen-Chari, southeastern Chad, fed by the Bahr Salamat; documented in 19th–20th century geography, with no written attestation <= 867 CE.
b_iro.etymology_analysis: Natural hydronym of Lake Iro (Lac Iro) in southeastern Chad, associated with the surrounding Gula Iro community.
